title: The universities
hookLine: Paris grew from its cathedral school; Oxford and Bologna rose in the same age

lines: A PSALM ON AN OPEN BOOK.
A CLUE TO WHERE IT CAME FROM.
cards: An open book on a coat of arms, the arms of the University of Oxford, and written across its pages, Dominus illuminatio mea.

The words open a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?" A place well-known for lectures and libraries and examinations chose, for its badge, a line of prayer.
It's a clue to where the whole idea of a university came from.

teach.b: In the middle ages, bishops kept schools at their cathedrals to train clergy to read, to sing the liturgy and to understand scripture.
In Paris, the school by the cathedral of Notre-Dame drew teachers, and the teachers drew students, until the streets around were full of both.

In the cities, bakers and masons banded together into guilds to protect their trade. Teachers and students did the same. In Latin, such a sworn body could be called a universitas, a whole company of people bound together.

teach.h: A GUILD OF MASTERS AND STUDENTS.
teach.b: The masters of Paris, the students of Bologna and the scholars of Oxford organized this way, and won rights from popes and kings to govern themselves. A day there was built on two things.
The lecture: a master read a text aloud, line by line, and explained it.
And the disputation: a question was posed, the arguments against were stated fairly, then the master gave his answer and replied to each objection.

Some readers see Anselm's phrase from day eight hundred, faith seeking understanding, turned here into a daily routine. You didn't win by shouting. You had to state the other side fairly before you answered it.
Degrees, the lecture hall, the idea that a question deserves an argument: these grew in schools where theology was taught alongside law and medicine and the arts.
The friars from yesterday's story went to these towns to study and teach. Learning was treated as a way of loving God with the mind.

how: Catholic universities today, and the Church's own pontifical faculties, keep the medieval pairing of faith and study; Catholics speak of theology as faith seeking understanding.

games.q: you're a master in Paris. a student raises a strong objection to what you teach. what do you do?
o: tell him to be quiet and listen.
state his objection fairly, then give your answer and reply to it.
games.why: that was the disputation: objections stated fairly first, then the answer and a reply to each.

practice: Pick a hard question you've been avoiding, in your faith, your work or your life, and do what a disputation does: state the strongest case against your own view as fairly as you can, then let your answer come and see whether it meets the objection.
There's no need to finish. If you pray, begin with the psalm's line, the Lord is my light.

wordCard.voice: University. The universitas: a sworn company of masters and students, growing in cities like Paris from the schools beside the cathedrals. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a whole body, a sworn company. In the cities it meant a guild of masters or students.

carryVoice: Your line: faith builds schools. The week ran from the stones of San Damiano to the lecture hall. That's day eight hundred twelve.
